## Paper

## Abstract

Various proxy data agree on a shallow Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) during the last glacial maximum (LGM), extending down to 2000 m−2500 m depth, which is similar to the AMOC geometry projected by climate models over the 21st century with rising atmospheric CO2. The AMOC strength in the two climate states is insufficiently constrained. Here the Antarctic Bottom Water (AABW) and North Atlantic Deep Water (NADW) properties from proxy data and climate models are used to investigate their influences on the AMOC. It is primarily the AABW’s potential density that determines the AMOC depth in both the LGM and warming climate. Changes in the potential density of the AABW, and the density contrast between NADW and AABW affect the pathways via which NADW returns to the surface and provide a constraint on AMOC strength. This study emphasizes the importance of the Southern Ocean in the AMOC’s depth and strength across climate states.

---

## Introduction

The AMOC is part of the global Meridional Overturning Circulation (MOC), which is a major component of the climate system. In a zonally averaged view, the MOC can be divided according to the region of deep-water formation into the North Atlantic Deep Water (NADW) cell characterised by northward flow in the upper ocean and southward flow in the deep ocean1, and the Antarctic Bottom Water (AABW) cell with northward flowing water in the abyssal ocean below the NADW cell. Changes in the MOC have a major influence on global and regional climate variability over a wide range of time scales by storing and transporting heat, freshwater, carbon and nutrients2–6.

The Last Glacial Maximum (LGM, ~21,000 years before present) is one of the best documented periods by paleoclimate archives and helpful for understanding past climate change and carbon cycle7. During the LGM, the AMOC was shallower relative to the present-day AMOC by about 1000–1500 m, which is a robust feature inferred from various types of tracers such as δ13C, Cd/Ca, PO4 and εNd8–13. The AMOC strength derived from proxy data, however, exhibits a large uncertainty, inhibiting a complete picture of the AMOC during the LGM. It remains highly controversial as to whether the glacial AMOC was stronger14, comparable15,16 or weaker17–22 relative to the present-day AMOC.

Paleoclimate modelling during the last several years attempted to reproduce the AMOC during the LGM constrained by proxy data23–26. Climate models generally agree on a stronger glacial AMOC relative to the present-day AMOC, yet disagree widely on the depth of the overturning cell26 (Supplementary Fig. 1) due to misrepresentations of various processes associated with surface-buoyancy forcing and mixing in the ocean interior27–29. These deficiencies lower the confidence in the climate models and contribute to the uncertainty regarding the AMOC projections over the 21st century with rising atmospheric CO2 30.

In this study, we evaluate the simulated properties of the NADW and AABW in climate models simulations against glacial reconstructions through direct model-data comparison. We also explore the influences of an improved AABW in the models on the AMOC geometry through a set of dedicated numerical experiments. As changes in the density of deep waters potentially affect the pathways via which deep water returns to the surface, this set of experiments permit to assess the dependence of AMOC strength on various overturning pathways across climate states, eventually allowing to constrain AMOC strength with observation-based estimates of the pathways in both the LGM and warming climate.

---

## Results

Changes in the deep ocean revealed by proxies
Changes in the properties of the NADW and AABW influence the AMOC depth and strength31–34 and therefore became a central topic of paleoclimate modelling35. The potential density of seawater, which is a function of temperature, salinity and pressure, is a direct indicator for the properties of the NADW and AABW and hence could provide information about their influences on the AMOC36. We first discuss the mean temperature and salinity, and the climate-model biases relative to observations at Feni Drift, Bermuda Rise and Shona Rise (Fig. 1a) in pre-industrial simulations with the Kiel Climate Model (KCM, “Methods”) and climate models participating in the Paleoclimate Modelling Intercomparison Project (PMIP). Temperature and salinity at these locations reveal the approximate properties of the NADW and AABW36. Two pre-industrial simulations were conducted with the KCM: one (PI) is performed with the standard version and the other (PIres) with salinity in the deep Southern Ocean (south of 60°S and below 3250 m) relaxed to the Levitus’ salinity climatology (“Methods”, Supplementary Fig. 2). All simulations (KCM and PMIP) presented in this study are integrated for at least a few hundred years to reduce the effects of spin-up.

There are noticeable warm biases in the pre-industrial control integrations of a number of climate models amounting up to about 3°C in the temperatures at Feni Drift, Bermuda Rise and Shona Rise relative to the EN4.2.2 and WOA18 datasets (Fig. 1b–d). Yet the climatological mean salinity at the three sites is generally in good agreement with the observations (Fig. 1b–d). Overall, most PMIP models and the KCM reproduce reasonably well the potential density σ2 (contours in Fig. 1b–d), which is referenced to 2000 m depth, in the deep North Atlantic and Southern Ocean in the pre-industrial control integrations. Following the PMIP protocol, the LGM simulations with the KCM and the PMIP models are performed by implementing glacial boundary conditions including among others continental ice sheets, greenhouse gas concentrations and orbital parameters (Methods). The potential density σ2 in the LGM simulations is significantly underestimated compared to the proxy data at the three sites (Fig. 1e–g). At Feni Drift and Bermuda Rise, the bias in σ2 can be mainly attributed to a warm temperature and to a lesser extent fresh salinity bias. The biased potential density at Shona Rise is largely related to fresh salinity biases in the deep Southern Ocean. Fresh biases there exceed 1 practical salinity unit (psu) in the LGM simulations performed with the standard KCM (Methods) and the PMIP models. We note that the salinity bias at Shona Rise in FGOLAS-g2 and MIROC-ESM exceeds 2 psu. This is likely because these models do not fully implement the PMIP protocol and do not add 1 psu to the oceanic initial conditions of the LGM simulations. The two CESM2 models show relatively dense waters at Shona Rise, which may be due to the parameterisation of density-driven overflow that moves dense water from the shelves to the deep ocean without cascading37,38.

Southern Ocean controls the geometry of the AMOC
The σ2 of the NADW and AABW at their source regions is suggested to be a major factor controlling the AMOC in the LGM and modern climate26,28,39,40. We examine the relationship of the AMOC in the region 20°S-10°N to the σ2 of the NADW and AABW. Here the AMOC depth is defined as the depth at which the overturning stream function is zero. The density of the NADW and AABW is represented by the vertical and area-weighted mean from 800 m to 2800 m over 50°N-55°N and 50°W-10°W in the North Atlantic, and below 3000m over 50°S-55°S and 50°W-10°E in the South Atlantic, respectively (yellow rectangles in Fig. 1a). The AMOC depth exhibits a statistically significant correlation of 0.70 at the 95% confidence level with the σ2 contrast between NADW and AABW in the LGM simulations (Fig. 2a). The significance of correlation coefficient is tested using the p value approach. It is primarily the σ2 of the AABW that exhibits a strong relationship with the AMOC depth, with a correlation of −0.71 (Fig. 2b). The NADW hardly influences the AMOC depth, as illustrated by its small and insignificant correlation with σ2 (not shown). Clearly, the shoaling of the AMOC in the LGM relative to the pre-industrial simulations is linked to enhanced stratification due to the rather dense AABW in the deep ocean36.

The AMOC is projected to shoal under enhanced greenhouse-gas forcing in the models participating in the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 6 (CMIP6)30. We examine the influence of the AABW density on the AMOC geometry in 90 global warming simulations under the Shared Socioeconomic Pathway 5–8.5 (SSP5-8.5) from 25 CMIP6 ensembles41,42 (Table 1, Supplementary Fig. 3). The individual members in each ensemble start from different atmospheric and oceanic initial conditions covering a wide range of climate states. We compute from all available ensemble members the mean AMOC depth between 20°S-10°N and the σ2 of the NADW and AABW averaged over the years 2071-2100. Similar to the LGM, the density contrast between the NADW and AABW exhibits a statistically significant correlation with the AMOC depth under global warming, which, however, is smaller amounting to 0.46 (Fig. 2c). Again, the σ2 of the AABW is the dominating factor determining the AMOC depth with a correlation of −0.72 (Fig. 2d), while the correlation with the σ2 of the NADW is again small and insignificant (not shown).

Improved North Atlantic surface climate due to reduced salinity bias in the Southern Ocean
The KCM suffers from systematic model biases in the North Atlantic as other PMIP models (Supplementary Fig. 4). To alleviate the impact of systematic biases, we compute the simulated SST responses in the LGM simulations relative to the pre-industrial experiment. The KCM’s response of sea surface temperature (SST) over the North Atlantic benefits from the reduced σ2 bias in the Southern Ocean. The late-winter mean (January-March, JFM) SST changes during the LGM from MARGO46, which is a proxy-based reconstruction for the glacial ocean conditions, depict a cooling pattern relative to the modern climate over the eastern North Atlantic, which extends from 60°N to 40°N (Fig. 4a). In comparison to MARGO, the standard KCM simulates a weaker response of cooling in the eastern North Atlantic that is restricted to north of 50°N from 35°W to 5°W (Fig. 4b). Correcting the salinity bias in the deep Southern Ocean in the experiment LGMres20, not only improves the AMOC but also broadens the meridional extent of the cooling in the eastern North Atlantic (Fig. 4c). Relative to MARGO, the root-mean-square-error averaged over 40°N-60°N and 35°W-5°W reduces from 5.32°C to 3.87°C in the restoring experiment. Consistently, the restoring experiment exhibits improvements in the simulated JFM mean SST compared to MARGO (Supplementary Fig. 5). We note that there are still some significant discrepancies in the SST-cooling response between MARGO and the salinity-restoring experiment, which may partly arise from the mean-state biases over the North Atlantic associated with deficiencies in the dynamical processes in the pre-industrial simulation with the KCM47. There is an eastward expansion of the sea ice associated with the cooling over the North Atlantic in LGMres20 (Fig. 4d–f), which reduces the local surface-heat flux and wind-driven oceanic salt transport29. As a result, the deep oceanic convection, as measured by the JFM mean mixed layer depth, is weakened south of Iceland in LGMres20 relative to the standard LGM simulation (Fig. 4g–i). We note that LGMres10 and LGMres15 show similar but smaller changes as LGMres20.

Dependence of changes in the glacial AMOC on the overturning pathways
One remaining issue is the strength of the glacial AMOC. As proxy data disagree on the changes in the AMOC strength during the LGM, we seek to constrain the AMOC changes using present-day observations, which is similar to the concept of emergent constraints48. This approach assumes that despite major differences among the climate models, relationships between the present-day and glacial climate are implicit within the model solutions of the partial differential equations governing the physical processes and parameterisations. Thus, the relationship between the present-day constraint variable (x) and glacial change in AMOC (y) can be expressed as y=f(x)+ε where ε represents a negligible deviation from function f. The function f can be obtained through analysis of a diverse model ensemble with varying resolution and parameterisations, such as the PMIP/CMIP ensembles. This allows us to establish a relationship between the glacial AMOC changes and the pre-industrial overturning pathways, where the pathways are quantified by the overturning streamfunction, which stands for the zonally integrated volume transport that returns the NADW to the surface (Methods).

In latitude-depth space, the AMOC can be regarded as a superposition of the shallower adiabatic cell and the deeper diabatic cell separated in the Atlantic and the Indo-Pacific basin. An acceleration (deceleration) of either cell strengthens (weakens) the AMOC. As suggested by Cessi (2019)49, about half of the volume of the modern NADW returns adiabatically to the surface through the wind-driven upwelling pathway in the Southern Ocean50 (SO_Windtotal). The remaining half of the NADW completes its circulation diabetically via diffusive upwelling in the Atlantic (Atdiffu) and Indo-Pacific51 (IPdiffu).

There is compelling evidence from modern hydrography that ageostrophic inter-basin transport connects the Atlantic with the Indo-Pacific, resulting from differences in the isopycnal depth on the order of 100 m between the two basins52. Specifically, analysis of water mass properties shows that the NADW rising to the surface of the Southern Ocean is transformed into AABW and then transported to the bottom of the Indo-Pacific. These dense waters are upwelled through diapycnal mixing and eventually return to the Atlantic1.

Each overturning pathway exhibits a large spread among the PMIP and CMIP models. Motivated by the influence of deep waters on the AMOC, we investigate relationships of the overturning pathways with the potential density of the NADW and AABW (Fig. 5). The Southern Ocean wind-driven pathway is positively correlated to the potential density contrast between the NADW and AABW in the LGM simulations (Fig. 5a). The correlation coefficient amounts to 0.62, which is significant at the 95% confidence level. Consistent with the LGM simulations, the potential density contrast between the NADW and AABW is associated with the magnitude of the Southern Ocean wind-driven pathway under global warming in CMIP simulations, with a correlation of 0.42 that is significant at the 95% confidence level (Fig. 5c).

The Indo-Pacific diffusive pathway exhibits no significant dependence on the potential density of the NADW and AABW in the LGM simulations with the PMIP models (blue lines Fig. 5b). Salinity-restoring experiments with the KCM suggest that enhanced potential density in the Atlantic basin tends to weaken the Indo-Pacific pathway (green lines in Fig. 5b). In contrast, global warming simulations with the CMIP6 models exhibits a positive correlation of the Indo-Pacific diffusive pathway with the potential density of the AABW, amounting to 0.53 which is significant at the 99% confidence level (Fig. 5d). Differences in the influence of the AABW on the Indo-Pacific diffusive pathway across the glacial and warming climate states are likely associated with the boundary conditions, particularly in the Northern Hemisphere. In summary, the two overturning pathways exhibit a significant relationship to the potential density of the AABW and NADW in the models across climate states.

Then each of the two pathways is examined with respect to the response of the AMOC strength, defined as the change in the LGM simulation relative to the pre-industrial simulation. Models with strong pre-industrial Southern Ocean wind-driven pathway tend to exhibit strengthened glacial AMOC driven by intensified westerly winds (Supplementary Fig 6), as indicated by the positive correlation (r=0.58), explaining about one third of the total variance among the models (PMIP and KCM, Fig. 6a). PMIP models with a stronger pre-industrial Indo-Pacific diffusive pathway are sensitive to the reduced inter-basin transport, which is affected by the glacial ocean stratification and depict an opposite relationship with the glacial AMOC response (r=−0.54; PMIP and KCM, Fig. 6b). Furthermore, the Indo-Pacific diffusive pathway is highly correlated with the glacial AMOC response (r=0.8, PMIP and KCM; Supplementary Fig 7c), consistent with previous studies53–55.

The above results suggest that the Southern Ocean wind-driven and the Indo-Pacific diffusive pathway can be used as a constraint on the glacial AMOC response. This hypothesis is tested using 110 global warming simulations from 12 CMIP5 (Table 2, Supplementary Fig 8) and 25 CMIP6 ensembles (Table 1, Supplementary Fig 3) employing the SSP5-8.5 scenario. The ensemble mean is computed using all available members and the model data are averaged over the years 2071–2100. Consistent with the LGM simulations, the weakening of the AMOC under global warming is dependent on the magnitude of the Southern Ocean wind-driven and Indo-Pacific diffusive pathways in the pre-industrial simulations (Fig. 6c, d). In particular, the Indo-Pacific diffusive pathway plays a dominant role in the AMOC response to global warming, explaining about 50% of the variance among the CMIP models (Fig. 6d). The weakening of the AMOC under global warming is largely attributed to the restricted Indian Ocean inflow induced by the shoaling of the AMOC56 and compensated by the Southern Ocean pathway driven by the intensified westerly winds (Supplementary Fig 6). We note that the CMIP6 models exhibit a stronger dependence of the AMOC response on the pre-industrial pathways than the CMIP5 models. This could be due to improvements in ocean stratification and abyssal circulation in the CMIP6 models57.

Stronger glacial AMOC revealed by observational-based estimates
Since the responses of glacial AMOC in the models exhibits a dependence on the pre-industrial Southern Ocean wind-driven as well as Indo-Pacific diffusive pathway, we use this dependence, as represented by linear regression, to estimate the glacial AMOC strength (Fig. 6a, b). Two global ocean-reanalysis systems employing state-of-the-art data assimilation are used to compute the present-day constraining variables: GloRanV1458 and ECCOv459. As shown in Fig. 6a, the dependence of the glacial AMOC response (y) on the pre-industrial Southern Ocean wind-driven pathway (x) can be simplified as y=0.85*x−3.31 using linear regression (green lines in Fig. 6a). The transport by the Southern Ocean wind-driven pathway amounts to 7.6 Sv (GloRanV14) and 14.0 Sv (ECCOv4). Substituting estimates for the Southern Ocean wind-driven pathway in the above constraint relationship, we obtain positive changes of the glacial AMOC amounting to 3.2 Sv (GloRanV14) and 8.6 Sv (ECCOv4). Both reanalysis datasets suggest a stronger glacial AMOC relative to the pre-industrial state (Fig. 6a). Similarly, regression analysis in Fig. 6b shows the constraint relationship between changes in the glacial AMOC and the present-day Indo-Pacific diffusive pathway as y=−0.82*x+9.13 (green lines in Fig. 6b). The transport by the Indo-Pacific diffusive pathway in GloRanV14 amounts to 8.1 Sv averaged over the years 2000–2021. In ECCOv4, the transport is 0.0 Sv60 averaged over the years 1992–2015. Both datasets reveal a stronger glacial AMOC relative to its pre-industrial state, with a large uncertainty ranging from 2.5 Sv (GloRanV14) to 9.1 Sv (ECCOv4) (Fig. 6b). A stronger glacial AMOC is consistent with enhanced surface-buoyancy forcing27,61,62 over the oceanic deep convection regions63 and also with previous studies employing isotope modelling64.

---

## Methods

Observational datasets and proxy reconstruction
To quantify the temperature and salinity biases of NADW and AABW in modern and glacial simulations, model results are compared to the present-day observations and to palaeoceanographic reconstructions, respectively. To obtain the mean-state salinity and temperature biases in pre-industrial simulations, the monthly version of EN4.2.2 objectively analysed temperature and salinity with bias corrections using the method of Cowley et al.79 is used as reference. Cowley et al. analyses and compares the ocean temperature profiles measured by some 4100 side-by-side deployed expendable bathythermographs and conductivity–temperature–depths such that the measurement biases in ocean temperature can be separated from those in depth. Biases in ocean temperature and salinity relative to the climatology from Volume I and Volume II of the World Ocean Atlas80,81 (WOA18) are considered as well. The temperature and salinity climatology of EN4.2.2 and WOA18 are both averaged over the period 1975–2004. The temperature and salinity biases during the LGM are mainly estimated by comparing the model data to proxy reconstructions at two sites from Ocean Drilling Program by Adkins et al.36.

Two reanalysis datasets, ECCOv4 and GloRanV14, are used here. Forced by the ERA-Interim data over the period 1992–2015, ECCOv4 uses a general circulation model (MITgcm) and assimilates most of available satellite and in-situ data. The data includes satellite sea surface height, ocean bottom pressure, sea surface temperature, sea surface salinity, in-situ temperature and salinity and sea-ice measurements from satellite and in-situ observations. The state estimation uses the adjoint method to iteratively minimise the squared sum of weighted model data misfits and control adjustments. The horizontal resolution varies from 22 km to 110 km, with the highest resolution in high latitudes and lowest resolution in mid latitudes.

GloRanV14 uses the eddy-permitting (1/4° horizontal resolution) Nucleus for European Modelling of the Ocean (NEMO) model, driven with atmospheric forcing from ERA-Interim over the period 1993–2021. Satellite sea surface height, sea surface temperature, sea-ice concentrations and in situ temperature and salinity are assimilated.

We choose the Multiproxy Approach for the Reconstruction of the Glacial Ocean Surface Project (MARGO) to estimate the sea surface temperature biases over the North Atlantic during the LGM46. The MARGO synthesis compiles and integrates 696 reconstructions of SSTs based on four microfossil (i.e. planktonic foraminifera, diatom, dinoflagellate cyst and radiolarian abundances) and two geochemical (alkenones and planktonic foraminifera Mg/Ca) proxies for the LGM. The geological age is rigorously defined as the period between 23 and 19 thousand years before present. This multiproxy approach yields the least biased representation for the glacial ocean conditions. The MARGO data are mapped on a global 5°×5° grid. The spatial coverage of proxies is especially dense in the North Atlantic, the Southern Ocean and the tropics. The samples in the subtropical gyres, especially in the Pacific Ocean, however, remain rare.

Kiel Climate Model and experimental setup
The simulations are carried out with a fully coupled atmosphere-ocean-sea ice general circulation model, the Kiel Climate Model82 (KCM). The version of the KCM used here consists of the ECHAM583 atmosphere general circulation model with a horizontal resolution of T42 (2.8°×2.8°), and with 19 vertical levels reaching up to 10 hPa. The atmosphere model is coupled to the NEMO-LIM ocean–sea ice model84 through the OASIS3 coupler85. The horizontal resolution of NEMO is approximately 2° (ORCA2 grid), with a meridional refinement of ~0.5° near the equator and 31 vertical levels.

The KCM suffers from biases in the abyssal ocean which are common to many climate models (Supplementary Fig 9a–c). Yet our aim is to investigate the influences of the abyssal biases on the AMOC, but not their causes. Here we investigate the impact of correcting the AABW salinity biases on the geometry and strength of the glacial AMOC. This is achieved by restoring the AABW salinity towards the palaeoceanographic salinity reconstructed by Adkins et al.36.

The experimental strategy is as follows: we perform two sets of experiments. The first set is performed with the standard KCM, which consists of two experiments: one 5300-year-long pre-industrial control run (PI) that is initialised with the Levitus climatology of temperature and salinity. Pre-industrial greenhouse gases, modern land-sea mask and continental ice-sheet geometry are employed in PI. In the other 5750-year-long simulation (LGM), the boundary conditions including greenhouse gas concentrations and orbital parameters are implemented in accordance with the PMIP4 protocol for the LGM experiments86. The LGM is initialised from the Levitus temperature climatology and salinity climatology to which 1 psu has been added to account for the 116-m drop of global mean sea level during the LGM. The simulated interactions between the tropical Pacific and the North Atlantic, and the multidecadal variability of the AMOC in LGM have been addressed in previous studies87,88.

For the second set of experiments, we apply a three-dimensional relaxation sponge in the Southern Ocean, south of 60°S (Supplementary Fig 2) following the configuration used by Patara and Böning89. As the KCM features strong mixing due to its coarse horizontal and vertical resolution, a relatively strong restoring has to be applied with a relaxation time set to 60 days. To avoid spurious sources of vorticity, the sponge area is restricted away from the Antarctic coast and its northern boundary. The relaxation weakens exponentially in the vicinity of rigid boundaries using the default smoothing function in NEMO. The first experiment (PIres) is a 1100-year-long pre-industrial run starting from the Levitus climatology, yet the salinity below approximately 3250-m in the Southern Ocean (south of 60°S) is restored to monthly values from the Levitus climatology. Notably, the salinity relaxation induces a small deficit in the freshwater budget. We therefore compute the seasonal cycle of the deficit using the initial 300-year monthly data and add the freshwater flux at the surface south of 60°S (Supplementary Fig 10). The zonal mean salinity bias in PIres slightly reduces relative to PI (Supplementary Fig 9). Yet the simulated mean climate and AMOC in PIres remain quite similar to those in PI (not shown). Three additional experiments under the LGM boundary conditions are performed. The salinity in the deep Southern Ocean is restored to monthly salinity climatology from the LGM simulation, to which 1.0 psu (LGMres10), 1.5 psu (LGMres15) or 2.0 psu (LGMres20) is added. Each simulation is integrated for 1600 years, such that the simulated mean climate and circulation reach a quasi-equilibrium state. The last 300-year monthly output from the two sets of simulations are used in the analysis shown here.

Calculation of overturning pathways
As palaeoceanographic reconstructions do not agree on the strength of the glacial AMOC, we seek for alternate ways, such as wind-driven and vertical diffusive processes, to constrain changes in the AMOC strength50,51,60. In the present-day overturning circulation, NADW returns to the ocean surface via either upwelling in the Southern Ocean forced by the westerly winds, or upwelling in the Atlantic and the Indo-Pacific Oceans through vertical diapycnal mixing. In particular, diffusive upwelling in the Indo-Pacific Ocean may significantly impact the global overturning circulation and hence, largely determines the responses of the AMOC strength to anthropogenic global warming in CMIP6 simulations60.

Similarly, we estimate the wind- and diffusion-driven overturning pathways to assess changes in the AMOC during the LGM. Following Baker et al.60, we use streamfunction, which represents the zonally integrated volume transport by Eulerian-mean and parameterised eddy velocity, as a measure for the overturning pathways. The pathways are defined by the processes and regions associated with this upwelling.

In CMIP6 models they can be estimated as follows,
Atdiffu=AMOCmax−AMOCmin (1)
SO_Windtotal=ψjϕ=34.5S (2)
To conserve the total volume of NADW, the diffusive pathway in the Indo-Pacific Ocean can be computed as the residual,
IPdiffu=AMOCmax−Atdiffu−SO_Windtotal, (3)
where AMOCmax represents the total volume of NADW and is defined as the maximum streamfunction in the North Atlantic. AMOCmin represents the NADW entering the Southern Ocean, which is quantified as the minimum streamfunction located between 34.5°S and the latitude of maximum streamfunction in the Atlantic basin. The difference between AMOCmax and AMOCmin thus represents the upwelled NADW via diffusive upwelling in the Atlantic. The total Southern Ocean wind-driven pathway (SO_Windtotal) is defined as the maximum global overturning streamfunciton located at approximately 34.5°S. The Indo-Pacific pathway is the residual arising from volume conservation.

## Your Original Review (Round 1)

### Reviewer 1

# Overall Assesment:
Thank you for the opportunity to review this manuscript. The paper demonstrates several strengths, including a systematic
approach to synthesizing multiple model results and a focused exploration of AMOC variability across different time-scales.
These aspects provide valuable insights into climate model behavior under different conditions, particularly regarding the
LGM and future projections. The topic addressed in this paper is indeed important, and I appreciate the effort the authors
have put into their work. However, after a thorough evaluation, I believe that the manuscript, in its current form, does not meet
the necessary standards for publication in Nature Communications. Below, I provide detailed comments to explain the
reasons for my decision and suggestions that the authors may consider for future revisions or resubmissions elsewhere.
# Major Concerns:
## Scientific Validity
The paper’s systematic synthesis of model outputs is valuable, yet key questions remain regarding the scientific impact of its
main findings. Clarifying why the contributions of Southern Ocean wind pathways and Indo-Pacific diffusion pathways differ
between the Last Glacial Maximum (LGM) and future projections would enhance the study's contribution. As demonstrated
in [e.g., Oka et al., 2021, Commun. Earth Env.], the Southern Ocean plays a crucial role in reproducing MOC during glacial
periods, highlighting the need to address such dynamics carefully. Additionally, further discussion on how this study
advances the understanding provided by Baker’s findings, and the reasons behind discrepancies in AMOC strength
estimations across datasets, would strengthen the paper and better situate it within the broader scientific literature.
## Methodological Issues
A primary concern is that the AMOC under preindustrial conditions in your model appears weaker than what observational
constraints would suggest, raising the question of whether this discrepancy might impact your results. Additionally, how did
AMOC vary between PI and PIres? Extended Figure 6 indicates that in PIres, a high salinity bias in the Southern Ocean’s
surface layer extends into lower latitudes.

The article at hand explores the key factors influencing the geometry and strength of the Atlantic Meridional Overturning
Circulation (AMOC) under different climate conditions—namely, the Last Glacial Maximum (LGM), the present-day climate,
and under global warming. The authors conclude that the potential density in the deep Southern Ocean plays a pivotal role
in realistically simulating the depth of the AMOC, highlighting its importance for understanding past and future AMOC
dynamics. However, several aspects of the study warrant closer scrutiny, particularly in terms of its treatment of stratification
processes in the Atlantic Ocean and the broader mechanisms influencing AMOC strength.
The deep-water formation during the Last Glacial Maximum (LGM) has been widely discussed in the paleoclimate literature.
Studies suggest that North Atlantic Deep Water (NADW) formation was shallower but not significantly weaker (Butzin et al.,
2005; Curry and Oppo, 2005; Duplessy et al., 1988). In contrast, Antarctic Bottom Water (AABW) export from the Southern
Ocean increased (Ledbetter and Johnson, 1976; Negre et al., 2010). Glacial AABW may have been saltier than today,
enhancing ocean stratification (Adkins et al., 2002; Bouttes et al., 2009). Modeling studies indicate that the shoaling of the
glacial AMOC was likely driven by changes in Southern Ocean sea ice (Baker et al., 2020; Ferrari et al., 2014) or freshwater
input from ice sheets (Miller et al., 2012).
Strengths
The article successfully builds on recent advancements in climate modeling to emphasize the crucial role of the Southern
Ocean in shaping the AMOC. It synthesizes various modeling studies to show that factors like wind-driven circulation in the
Southern Ocean and diffusive pathways in the Indo-Pacific are key to understanding AMOC responses to different climate
states. This focus on Southern Ocean dynamics aligns with recent literature, including the findings of Heuzé et al., which
highlight the importance of shelf processes and density-driven overflows in shaping Antarctic Bottom Water (AABW)
characteristics. The paper’s quantitative approach, calculating correlations between model responses and major present-
day overturning pathways, is an important contribution to narrowing down uncertainties in predicting glacial AMOC strength.
Additionally, the comparison of CMIP5 and CMIP6 models is a strength, as it identifies key model improvements—such as
better vertical diffusion and mesoscale eddies representation—which contribute to a more accurate depiction of the AMOC.
This is a relevant aspect, given the continued evolution of climate modeling capabilities and the need for more robust
simulations of oceanic processes at various spatiotemporal scales.
Weaknesses
While the article makes a contribution to the understanding of AMOC dynamics under LGM conditions, it glosses over
important aspects that could refine its conclusions. A key omission is the lack of detailed discussion on the vertical
stratification of the Atlantic Ocean, a mechanism that plays a critical role in modulating AMOC strength during the glacial
period. This gap is particularly notable given that studies like those of Adkins et al., 2002; Knorr et al., 2021; Chen et al.,
2024 have argued that a stronger stratification during the LGM was a critical factor for the shoaling of the AMOC.
Specifically, they suggest that the salinity of glacial deep waters, which offset the effect of their warmer temperatures, is
crucial for understanding changes in density and, by extension, the depth and strength of the AMOC. Chen et al. further
argue that strong glacial-ocean stratification, independent of tidal dissipation, was primarily responsible for the shoaled
AMOC during the glacial period.
As one aim is to investigate the influences of the abyssal biases on the AMOC, one might look onto earlier papers analyzing
the effect of Southern Ocean warming (Zhang et al., 2013, CP, also discussing PMIP). Similar sensitivity experiments under
the LGM boundary with restoring were already performed earlier, but it is not mentioned. Indeed, a salty deep ocean is found
to be a prerequisite for glacial termination (Knorr et al., 2021, Nat Geo), see also Extended Data Fig. 10: Glacial Atlantic
salinity structure in models of the last three PMIP/CMIP generations.
Moreover, the paper does not engage deeply with the interactions between different ocean basins, particularly the Atlantic
and Indo-Pacific. While the correlation between the Southern Ocean wind-driven and Indo-Pacific diffusive pathways is
presented, there is limited discussion of the mechanisms by which these pathways interact to influence the AMOC. Given
the complex nature of ocean circulation, particularly in the Southern Ocean, a more detailed treatment of how these
processes interlink would strengthen the authors' argument. My feeling is that this aspect is the truly innovative one.
As a more minor Conceptual Gaps and Uncertainties: The authors’ reliance on model correlations to constrain AMOC
strength is also problematic because it assumes that the relationships observed in modern climate states are fully
transferable to the glacial period. The LGM represents a unique set of conditions—such as the presence of large ice sheets,
altered atmospheric circulation patterns, and reduced CO₂ concentrations—that may have influenced AMOC dynamics in
ways that are not captured by present-day pathways. This introduces an additional layer of uncertainty that is not fully
addressed.
Conclusion
In conclusion, while the article provides a contribution to our understanding of the AMOC under different climate states, it is
limited by its under-exploration of vertical stratification in the Atlantic Ocean, its reliance on uncertain present-day analogs
for constraining glacial AMOC strength, and its insufficient treatment of the interactions between different ocean basins. The
study would benefit from a deeper examination of these processes, particularly the role of glacial ocean stratification (some
references are given above) and interbasin linkages, to provide a more comprehensive and accurate picture of AMOC
variability across past, present, and future climate states.

## Paper

## Abstract

Various proxy data agree on a shallow Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) during the last glacial maximum (LGM), extending down to 2000 m−2500 m depth, which is similar to the AMOC geometry projected by climate models over the 21st century with rising atmospheric CO2. The AMOC strength in the two climate states is insufficiently constrained. Here the Antarctic Bottom Water (AABW) and North Atlantic Deep Water (NADW) properties from proxy data and climate models are used to investigate their influences on the AMOC. It is primarily the AABW’s potential density that determines the AMOC depth in both the LGM and warming climate. Changes in the potential density of the AABW, and the density contrast between NADW and AABW affect the pathways via which NADW returns to the surface and provide a constraint on AMOC strength. This study emphasizes the importance of the Southern Ocean in the AMOC’s depth and strength across climate states.

---

## Introduction

The AMOC is part of the global Meridional Overturning Circulation (MOC), which is a major component of the climate system. In a zonally averaged view, the MOC can be divided according to the region of deep-water formation into the North Atlantic Deep Water (NADW) cell characterised by northward flow in the upper ocean and southward flow in the deep ocean1, and the Antarctic Bottom Water (AABW) cell with northward flowing water in the abyssal ocean below the NADW cell. Changes in the MOC have a major influence on global and regional climate variability over a wide range of time scales by storing and transporting heat, freshwater, carbon and nutrients2–6.

The Last Glacial Maximum (LGM, ~21,000 years before present) is one of the best documented periods by paleoclimate archives and helpful for understanding past climate change and carbon cycle7. During the LGM, the AMOC was shallower relative to the present-day AMOC by about 1000–1500 m, which is a robust feature inferred from various types of tracers such as δ13C, Cd/Ca, PO4 and εNd8–13. The AMOC strength derived from proxy data, however, exhibits a large uncertainty, inhibiting a complete picture of the AMOC during the LGM. It remains highly controversial as to whether the glacial AMOC was stronger14, comparable15,16 or weaker17–22 relative to the present-day AMOC.

Paleoclimate modelling during the last several years attempted to reproduce the AMOC during the LGM constrained by proxy data23–26. Climate models generally agree on a stronger glacial AMOC relative to the present-day AMOC, yet disagree widely on the depth of the overturning cell26 (Supplementary Fig. 1) due to misrepresentations of various processes associated with surface-buoyancy forcing and mixing in the ocean interior27–29. These deficiencies lower the confidence in the climate models and contribute to the uncertainty regarding the AMOC projections over the 21st century with rising atmospheric CO2 30.

In this study, we evaluate the simulated properties of the NADW and AABW in climate models simulations against glacial reconstructions through direct model-data comparison. We also explore the influences of an improved AABW in the models on the AMOC geometry through a set of dedicated numerical experiments. As changes in the density of deep waters potentially affect the pathways via which deep water returns to the surface, this set of experiments permit to assess the dependence of AMOC strength on various overturning pathways across climate states, eventually allowing to constrain AMOC strength with observation-based estimates of the pathways in both the LGM and warming climate.

---

## Results

Changes in the deep ocean revealed by proxies
Changes in the properties of the NADW and AABW influence the AMOC depth and strength31–34 and therefore became a central topic of paleoclimate modelling35. The potential density of seawater, which is a function of temperature, salinity and pressure, is a direct indicator for the properties of the NADW and AABW and hence could provide information about their influences on the AMOC36. We first discuss the mean temperature and salinity, and the climate-model biases relative to observations at Feni Drift, Bermuda Rise and Shona Rise (Fig. 1a) in pre-industrial simulations with the Kiel Climate Model (KCM, “Methods”) and climate models participating in the Paleoclimate Modelling Intercomparison Project (PMIP). Temperature and salinity at these locations reveal the approximate properties of the NADW and AABW36. Two pre-industrial simulations were conducted with the KCM: one (PI) is performed with the standard version and the other (PIres) with salinity in the deep Southern Ocean (south of 60°S and below 3250 m) relaxed to the Levitus’ salinity climatology (“Methods”, Supplementary Fig. 2). All simulations (KCM and PMIP) presented in this study are integrated for at least a few hundred years to reduce the effects of spin-up.

There are noticeable warm biases in the pre-industrial control integrations of a number of climate models amounting up to about 3°C in the temperatures at Feni Drift, Bermuda Rise and Shona Rise relative to the EN4.2.2 and WOA18 datasets (Fig. 1b–d). Yet the climatological mean salinity at the three sites is generally in good agreement with the observations (Fig. 1b–d). Overall, most PMIP models and the KCM reproduce reasonably well the potential density σ2 (contours in Fig. 1b–d), which is referenced to 2000 m depth, in the deep North Atlantic and Southern Ocean in the pre-industrial control integrations. Following the PMIP protocol, the LGM simulations with the KCM and the PMIP models are performed by implementing glacial boundary conditions including among others continental ice sheets, greenhouse gas concentrations and orbital parameters (Methods). The potential density σ2 in the LGM simulations is significantly underestimated compared to the proxy data at the three sites (Fig. 1e–g). At Feni Drift and Bermuda Rise, the bias in σ2 can be mainly attributed to a warm temperature and to a lesser extent fresh salinity bias. The biased potential density at Shona Rise is largely related to fresh salinity biases in the deep Southern Ocean. Fresh biases there exceed 1 practical salinity unit (psu) in the LGM simulations performed with the standard KCM (Methods) and the PMIP models. We note that the salinity bias at Shona Rise in FGOLAS-g2 and MIROC-ESM exceeds 2 psu. This is likely because these models do not fully implement the PMIP protocol and do not add 1 psu to the oceanic initial conditions of the LGM simulations. The two CESM2 models show relatively dense waters at Shona Rise, which may be due to the parameterisation of density-driven overflow that moves dense water from the shelves to the deep ocean without cascading37,38.

Southern Ocean controls the geometry of the AMOC
The σ2 of the NADW and AABW at their source regions is suggested to be a major factor controlling the AMOC in the LGM and modern climate26,28,39,40. We examine the relationship of the AMOC in the region 20°S-10°N to the σ2 of the NADW and AABW. Here the AMOC depth is defined as the depth at which the overturning stream function is zero. The density of the NADW and AABW is represented by the vertical and area-weighted mean from 800 m to 2800 m over 50°N-55°N and 50°W-10°W in the North Atlantic, and below 3000m over 50°S-55°S and 50°W-10°E in the South Atlantic, respectively (yellow rectangles in Fig. 1a). The AMOC depth exhibits a statistically significant correlation of 0.70 at the 95% confidence level with the σ2 contrast between NADW and AABW in the LGM simulations (Fig. 2a). The significance of correlation coefficient is tested using the p value approach. It is primarily the σ2 of the AABW that exhibits a strong relationship with the AMOC depth, with a correlation of −0.71 (Fig. 2b). The NADW hardly influences the AMOC depth, as illustrated by its small and insignificant correlation with σ2 (not shown). Clearly, the shoaling of the AMOC in the LGM relative to the pre-industrial simulations is linked to enhanced stratification due to the rather dense AABW in the deep ocean36.

The AMOC is projected to shoal under enhanced greenhouse-gas forcing in the models participating in the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 6 (CMIP6)30. We examine the influence of the AABW density on the AMOC geometry in 90 global warming simulations under the Shared Socioeconomic Pathway 5–8.5 (SSP5-8.5) from 25 CMIP6 ensembles41,42 (Table 1, Supplementary Fig. 3). The individual members in each ensemble start from different atmospheric and oceanic initial conditions covering a wide range of climate states. We compute from all available ensemble members the mean AMOC depth between 20°S-10°N and the σ2 of the NADW and AABW averaged over the years 2071-2100. Similar to the LGM, the density contrast between the NADW and AABW exhibits a statistically significant correlation with the AMOC depth under global warming, which, however, is smaller amounting to 0.46 (Fig. 2c). Again, the σ2 of the AABW is the dominating factor determining the AMOC depth with a correlation of −0.72 (Fig. 2d), while the correlation with the σ2 of the NADW is again small and insignificant (not shown).

Improved North Atlantic surface climate due to reduced salinity bias in the Southern Ocean
The KCM suffers from systematic model biases in the North Atlantic as other PMIP models (Supplementary Fig. 4). To alleviate the impact of systematic biases, we compute the simulated SST responses in the LGM simulations relative to the pre-industrial experiment. The KCM’s response of sea surface temperature (SST) over the North Atlantic benefits from the reduced σ2 bias in the Southern Ocean. The late-winter mean (January-March, JFM) SST changes during the LGM from MARGO46, which is a proxy-based reconstruction for the glacial ocean conditions, depict a cooling pattern relative to the modern climate over the eastern North Atlantic, which extends from 60°N to 40°N (Fig. 4a). In comparison to MARGO, the standard KCM simulates a weaker response of cooling in the eastern North Atlantic that is restricted to north of 50°N from 35°W to 5°W (Fig. 4b). Correcting the salinity bias in the deep Southern Ocean in the experiment LGMres20, not only improves the AMOC but also broadens the meridional extent of the cooling in the eastern North Atlantic (Fig. 4c). Relative to MARGO, the root-mean-square-error averaged over 40°N-60°N and 35°W-5°W reduces from 5.32°C to 3.87°C in the restoring experiment. Consistently, the restoring experiment exhibits improvements in the simulated JFM mean SST compared to MARGO (Supplementary Fig. 5). We note that there are still some significant discrepancies in the SST-cooling response between MARGO and the salinity-restoring experiment, which may partly arise from the mean-state biases over the North Atlantic associated with deficiencies in the dynamical processes in the pre-industrial simulation with the KCM47. There is an eastward expansion of the sea ice associated with the cooling over the North Atlantic in LGMres20 (Fig. 4d–f), which reduces the local surface-heat flux and wind-driven oceanic salt transport29. As a result, the deep oceanic convection, as measured by the JFM mean mixed layer depth, is weakened south of Iceland in LGMres20 relative to the standard LGM simulation (Fig. 4g–i). We note that LGMres10 and LGMres15 show similar but smaller changes as LGMres20.

Dependence of changes in the glacial AMOC on the overturning pathways
One remaining issue is the strength of the glacial AMOC. As proxy data disagree on the changes in the AMOC strength during the LGM, we seek to constrain the AMOC changes using present-day observations, which is similar to the concept of emergent constraints48. This approach assumes that despite major differences among the climate models, relationships between the present-day and glacial climate are implicit within the model solutions of the partial differential equations governing the physical processes and parameterisations. Thus, the relationship between the present-day constraint variable (x) and glacial change in AMOC (y) can be expressed as y=f(x)+ε where ε represents a negligible deviation from function f. The function f can be obtained through analysis of a diverse model ensemble with varying resolution and parameterisations, such as the PMIP/CMIP ensembles. This allows us to establish a relationship between the glacial AMOC changes and the pre-industrial overturning pathways, where the pathways are quantified by the overturning streamfunction, which stands for the zonally integrated volume transport that returns the NADW to the surface (Methods).

In latitude-depth space, the AMOC can be regarded as a superposition of the shallower adiabatic cell and the deeper diabatic cell separated in the Atlantic and the Indo-Pacific basin. An acceleration (deceleration) of either cell strengthens (weakens) the AMOC. As suggested by Cessi (2019)49, about half of the volume of the modern NADW returns adiabatically to the surface through the wind-driven upwelling pathway in the Southern Ocean50 (SO_Windtotal). The remaining half of the NADW completes its circulation diabetically via diffusive upwelling in the Atlantic (Atdiffu) and Indo-Pacific51 (IPdiffu).

There is compelling evidence from modern hydrography that ageostrophic inter-basin transport connects the Atlantic with the Indo-Pacific, resulting from differences in the isopycnal depth on the order of 100 m between the two basins52. Specifically, analysis of water mass properties shows that the NADW rising to the surface of the Southern Ocean is transformed into AABW and then transported to the bottom of the Indo-Pacific. These dense waters are upwelled through diapycnal mixing and eventually return to the Atlantic1.

Each overturning pathway exhibits a large spread among the PMIP and CMIP models. Motivated by the influence of deep waters on the AMOC, we investigate relationships of the overturning pathways with the potential density of the NADW and AABW (Fig. 5). The Southern Ocean wind-driven pathway is positively correlated to the potential density contrast between the NADW and AABW in the LGM simulations (Fig. 5a). The correlation coefficient amounts to 0.62, which is significant at the 95% confidence level. Consistent with the LGM simulations, the potential density contrast between the NADW and AABW is associated with the magnitude of the Southern Ocean wind-driven pathway under global warming in CMIP simulations, with a correlation of 0.42 that is significant at the 95% confidence level (Fig. 5c).

The Indo-Pacific diffusive pathway exhibits no significant dependence on the potential density of the NADW and AABW in the LGM simulations with the PMIP models (blue lines Fig. 5b). Salinity-restoring experiments with the KCM suggest that enhanced potential density in the Atlantic basin tends to weaken the Indo-Pacific pathway (green lines in Fig. 5b). In contrast, global warming simulations with the CMIP6 models exhibits a positive correlation of the Indo-Pacific diffusive pathway with the potential density of the AABW, amounting to 0.53 which is significant at the 99% confidence level (Fig. 5d). Differences in the influence of the AABW on the Indo-Pacific diffusive pathway across the glacial and warming climate states are likely associated with the boundary conditions, particularly in the Northern Hemisphere. In summary, the two overturning pathways exhibit a significant relationship to the potential density of the AABW and NADW in the models across climate states.

Then each of the two pathways is examined with respect to the response of the AMOC strength, defined as the change in the LGM simulation relative to the pre-industrial simulation. Models with strong pre-industrial Southern Ocean wind-driven pathway tend to exhibit strengthened glacial AMOC driven by intensified westerly winds (Supplementary Fig 6), as indicated by the positive correlation (r=0.58), explaining about one third of the total variance among the models (PMIP and KCM, Fig. 6a). PMIP models with a stronger pre-industrial Indo-Pacific diffusive pathway are sensitive to the reduced inter-basin transport, which is affected by the glacial ocean stratification and depict an opposite relationship with the glacial AMOC response (r=−0.54; PMIP and KCM, Fig. 6b). Furthermore, the Indo-Pacific diffusive pathway is highly correlated with the glacial AMOC response (r=0.8, PMIP and KCM; Supplementary Fig 7c), consistent with previous studies53–55.

The above results suggest that the Southern Ocean wind-driven and the Indo-Pacific diffusive pathway can be used as a constraint on the glacial AMOC response. This hypothesis is tested using 110 global warming simulations from 12 CMIP5 (Table 2, Supplementary Fig 8) and 25 CMIP6 ensembles (Table 1, Supplementary Fig 3) employing the SSP5-8.5 scenario. The ensemble mean is computed using all available members and the model data are averaged over the years 2071–2100. Consistent with the LGM simulations, the weakening of the AMOC under global warming is dependent on the magnitude of the Southern Ocean wind-driven and Indo-Pacific diffusive pathways in the pre-industrial simulations (Fig. 6c, d). In particular, the Indo-Pacific diffusive pathway plays a dominant role in the AMOC response to global warming, explaining about 50% of the variance among the CMIP models (Fig. 6d). The weakening of the AMOC under global warming is largely attributed to the restricted Indian Ocean inflow induced by the shoaling of the AMOC56 and compensated by the Southern Ocean pathway driven by the intensified westerly winds (Supplementary Fig 6). We note that the CMIP6 models exhibit a stronger dependence of the AMOC response on the pre-industrial pathways than the CMIP5 models. This could be due to improvements in ocean stratification and abyssal circulation in the CMIP6 models57.

Stronger glacial AMOC revealed by observational-based estimates
Since the responses of glacial AMOC in the models exhibits a dependence on the pre-industrial Southern Ocean wind-driven as well as Indo-Pacific diffusive pathway, we use this dependence, as represented by linear regression, to estimate the glacial AMOC strength (Fig. 6a, b). Two global ocean-reanalysis systems employing state-of-the-art data assimilation are used to compute the present-day constraining variables: GloRanV1458 and ECCOv459. As shown in Fig. 6a, the dependence of the glacial AMOC response (y) on the pre-industrial Southern Ocean wind-driven pathway (x) can be simplified as y=0.85*x−3.31 using linear regression (green lines in Fig. 6a). The transport by the Southern Ocean wind-driven pathway amounts to 7.6 Sv (GloRanV14) and 14.0 Sv (ECCOv4). Both datasets reveal a stronger glacial AMOC relative to its pre-industrial state, with a large uncertainty ranging from 2.5 Sv (GloRanV14) to 9.1 Sv (ECCOv4) (Fig. 6b). A stronger glacial AMOC is consistent with enhanced surface-buoyancy forcing27,61,62 over the oceanic deep convection regions63 and also with previous studies employing isotope modelling64.

## Methods

Observational datasets and proxy reconstruction
To quantify the temperature and salinity biases of NADW and AABW in modern and glacial simulations, model results are compared to the present-day observations and to palaeoceanographic reconstructions, respectively. To obtain the mean-state salinity and temperature biases in pre-industrial simulations, the monthly version of EN4.2.2 objectively analysed temperature and salinity with bias corrections using the method of Cowley et al.79 is used as reference. Cowley et al. analyses and compares the ocean temperature profiles measured by some 4100 side-by-side deployed expendable bathythermographs and conductivity–temperature–depths such that the measurement biases in ocean temperature can be separated from those in depth. Biases in ocean temperature and salinity relative to the climatology from Volume I and Volume II of the World Ocean Atlas80,81 (WOA18) are considered as well. The temperature and salinity climatology of EN4.2.2 and WOA18 are both averaged over the period 1975–2004. The temperature and salinity biases during the LGM are mainly estimated by comparing the model data to proxy reconstructions at two sites from Ocean Drilling Program by Adkins et al.36.

Two reanalysis datasets, ECCOv4 and GloRanV14, are used here. Forced by the ERA-Interim data over the period 1992–2015, ECCOv4 uses a general circulation model (MITgcm) and assimilates most of available satellite and in-situ data. The data includes satellite sea surface height, ocean bottom pressure, sea surface temperature, sea surface salinity, in-situ temperature and salinity and sea-ice measurements from satellite and in-situ observations. The state estimation uses the adjoint method to iteratively minimise the squared sum of weighted model data misfits and control adjustments. The horizontal resolution varies from 22 km to 110 km, with the highest resolution in high latitudes and lowest resolution in mid latitudes.

GloRanV14 uses the eddy-permitting (1/4° horizontal resolution) Nucleus for European Modelling of the Ocean (NEMO) model, driven with atmospheric forcing from ERA-Interim over the period 1993–2021. Satellite sea surface height, sea surface temperature, sea-ice concentrations and in situ temperature and salinity are assimilated.

We choose the Multiproxy Approach for the Reconstruction of the Glacial Ocean Surface Project (MARGO) to estimate the sea surface temperature biases over the North Atlantic during the LGM46. The MARGO synthesis compiles and integrates 696 reconstructions of SSTs based on four microfossil (i.e. planktonic foraminifera, diatom, dinoflagellate cyst and radiolarian abundances) and two geochemical (alkenones and planktonic foraminifera Mg/Ca) proxies for the LGM. The geological age is rigorously defined as the period between 23 and 19 thousand years before present. This multiproxy approach yields the least biased representation for the glacial ocean conditions. The MARGO data are mapped on a global 5°×5° grid. The spatial coverage of proxies is especially dense in the North Atlantic, the Southern Ocean and the tropics. The samples in the subtropical gyres, especially in the Pacific Ocean, however, remain rare.

Kiel Climate Model and experimental setup
The simulations are carried out with a fully coupled atmosphere-ocean-sea ice general circulation model, the Kiel Climate Model82 (KCM). The version of the KCM used here consists of the ECHAM583 atmosphere general circulation model with a horizontal resolution of T42 (2.8°×2.8°), and with 19 vertical levels reaching up to 10 hPa. The atmosphere model is coupled to the NEMO-LIM ocean–sea ice model84 through the OASIS3 coupler85. The horizontal resolution of NEMO is approximately 2° (ORCA2 grid), with a meridional refinement of ~0.5° near the equator and 31 vertical levels.

The KCM suffers from biases in the abyssal ocean which are common to many climate models (Supplementary Fig 9a–c). Yet our aim is to investigate the influences of the abyssal biases on the AMOC, but not their causes. Here we investigate the impact of correcting the AABW salinity biases on the geometry and strength of the glacial AMOC. This is achieved by restoring the AABW salinity towards the palaeoceanographic salinity reconstructed by Adkins et al.36.

The experimental strategy is as follows: we perform two sets of experiments. The first set is performed with the standard KCM, which consists of two experiments: one 5300-year-long pre-industrial control run (PI) that is initialised with the Levitus climatology of temperature and salinity. Pre-industrial greenhouse gases, modern land-sea mask and continental ice-sheet geometry are employed in PI. In the other 5750-year-long simulation (LGM), the boundary conditions including greenhouse gas concentrations and orbital parameters are implemented in accordance with the PMIP4 protocol for the LGM experiments86. The LGM is initialised from the Levitus temperature climatology and salinity climatology to which 1 psu has been added to account for the 116-m drop of global mean sea level during the LGM. The simulated interactions between the tropical Pacific and the North Atlantic, and the multidecadal variability of the AMOC in LGM have been addressed in previous studies87,88.

For the second set of experiments, we apply a three-dimensional relaxation sponge in the Southern Ocean, south of 60°S (Supplementary Fig 2) following the configuration used by Patara and Böning89. As the KCM features strong mixing due to its coarse horizontal and vertical resolution, a relatively strong restoring has to be applied with a relaxation time set to 60 days. To avoid spurious sources of vorticity, the sponge area is restricted away from the Antarctic coast and its northern boundary. The relaxation weakens exponentially in the vicinity of rigid boundaries using the default smoothing function in NEMO. The first experiment (PIres) is a 1100-year-long pre-industrial run starting from the Levitus climatology, yet the salinity below approximately 3250-m in the Southern Ocean (south of 60°S) is restored to monthly values from the Levitus climatology. Notably, the salinity relaxation induces a small deficit in the freshwater budget. We therefore compute the seasonal cycle of the deficit using the initial 300-year monthly data and add the freshwater flux at the surface south of 60°S (Supplementary Fig 10). The zonal mean salinity bias in PIres slightly reduces relative to PI (Supplementary Fig 9). Yet the simulated mean climate and AMOC in PIres remain quite similar to those in PI (not shown). Three additional experiments under the LGM boundary conditions are performed. The salinity in the deep Southern Ocean is restored to monthly salinity climatology from the LGM simulation, to which 1.0 psu (LGMres10), 1.5 psu (LGMres15) or 2.0 psu (LGMres20) is added. Each simulation is integrated for 1600 years, such that the simulated mean climate and circulation reach a quasi-equilibrium state. The last 300-year monthly output from the two sets of simulations are used in the analysis shown here.

As palaeoceanographic reconstructions do not agree on the strength of the glacial AMOC, we seek for alternate ways, such as wind-driven and vertical diffusive processes, to constrain changes in the AMOC strength50,51,60. In the present-day overturning circulation, NADW returns to the ocean surface via either upwelling in the Southern Ocean forced by the westerly winds, or upwelling in the Atlantic and the Indo-Pacific Oceans through vertical diapycnal mixing. In particular, diffusive upwelling in the Indo-Pacific Ocean may significantly impact the global overturning circulation and hence, largely determines the responses of the AMOC strength to anthropogenic global warming in CMIP6 simulations60.

Similarly, we estimate the wind- and diffusion-driven overturning pathways to assess changes in the AMOC during the LGM. Following Baker et al.60, we use streamfunction, which represents the zonally integrated volume transport by Eulerian-mean and parameterised eddy velocity, as a measure for the overturning pathways. The article at hand explores the key factors influencing the geometry and strength of the Atlantic Meridional Overturning

The deep-water formation during the Last Glacial Maximum (LGM) has been widely discussed in the paleoclimate literature.

Strengths
The article successfully builds on recent advancements in climate modeling to emphasize the crucial role of the Southern
Ocean in shaping the AMOC. It synthesizes various modeling studies to show that factors like wind-driven circulation in the
Southern Ocean and diffusive pathways in the Indo-Pacific are key to understanding AMOC responses to different climate
states. This focus on Southern Ocean dynamics aligns with recent literature, including the findings of Heuzé et al., which
highlight the importance of shelf processes and density-driven overflows in shaping Antarctic Bottom Water (AABW)
characteristics. The paper’s quantitative approach, calculating correlations between model responses and major present-
day overturning pathways, is an important contribution to narrowing down uncertainties in predicting glacial AMOC strength.

better vertical diffusion and mesoscale eddies representation—which contribute to a more accurate depiction of the AMOC.

simulations of oceanic processes at various spatiotemporal scales.

While the article makes a contribution to the understanding of AMOC dynamics under LGM conditions, it glosses over
important aspects that could refine its conclusions. A key omission is the lack of detailed discussion on the vertical
stratification of the Atlantic Ocean, a mechanism that plays a critical role in modulating AMOC strength during the glacial
period. This gap is particularly notable given that studies like those of Adkins et al., 2002; Knorr et al., 2021; Chen et al.,
2024 have argued that a stronger stratification during the LGM was a critical factor for the shoaling of the AMOC.

argue that strong glacial-ocean stratification, independent of tidal dissipation, was primarily responsible for the shoaled

strength is also problematic because it assumes that the relationships observed in modern climate states are fully
transferable to the glacial period. The LGM represents a unique set of conditions—such as the presence of large ice sheets,
altered atmospheric circulation patterns, and reduced CO₂ concentrations—that may have influenced AMOC dynamics in
ways that are not captured by present-day pathways. This introduces an additional layer of uncertainty that is not fully
addressed.

In conclusion, while the article provides a contribution to our understanding of the AMOC under different climate states, it is
limited by its under-exploration of vertical stratification in the Atlantic Ocean, its reliance on uncertain present-day analogs
for constraining glacial AMOC strength, and its insufficient treatment of the interactions between different ocean basins. The
study would benefit from a deeper examination of these processes, particularly the role of glacial ocean stratification (some

variability across past, present, and future climate states.

Reviewer #2
The article at hand explores the key factors influencing the geometry and strength of the
Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) under different climate conditions—namely,
the Last Glacial Maximum (LGM), the present-day climate, and under global warming. The
authors conclude that the potential density in the deep Southern Ocean plays a pivotal role in
realistically simulating the depth of the AMOC, highlighting its importance for understanding past
and future AMOC dynamics. However, several aspects of the study warrant closer scrutiny,
particularly in terms of its treatment of stratification processes in the Atlantic Ocean and the
broader mechanisms influencing AMOC strength.
The deep-water formation during the Last Glacial Maximum (LGM) has been widely
discussed in the paleoclimate literature. Studies suggest that North Atlantic Deep Water (NADW)
formation was shallower but not significantly weaker (Butzin et al., 2005; Curry and Oppo, 2005;
Duplessy et al., 1988). In contrast, Antarctic Bottom Water (AABW) export from the Southern
Ocean increased (Ledbetter and Johnson, 1976; Negre et al., 2010). Glacial AABW may have been
saltier than today, enhancing ocean stratification (Adkins et al., 2002; Bouttes et al., 2009). Modeling
studies indicate that the shoaling of the glacial AMOC was likely driven by changes in Southern
Ocean sea ice (Baker et al., 2020; Ferrari et al., 2014) or freshwater input from ice
sheets (Miller et al., 2012).
Strengths
The article successfully builds on recent advancements in climate modeling to emphasize
the crucial role of the Southern Ocean in shaping the AMOC. It synthesizes various modeling
studies to show that factors like wind-driven circulation in the Southern Ocean and diffusive
pathways in the Indo-Pacific are key to understanding AMOC responses to different climate states.
This focus on Southern Ocean dynamics aligns with recent literature, including the findings of
Heuzé et al., which highlight the importance of shelf processes and density-driven overflows in
shaping Antarctic Bottom Water (AABW) characteristics. The paper’s quantitative approach,
calculating correlations between model responses and major present-day overturning pathways,
is an important contribution to narrowing down uncertainties in predicting glacial AMOC strength.
Additionally, the comparison of CMIP5 and CMIP6 models is a strength, as it identifies key model
improvements—such as better vertical diffusion and mesoscale eddies representation—which
contribute to a more accurate depiction of the AMOC. This is a relevant aspect, given the continued
evolution of climate modeling capabilities and the need for more robust simulations of oceanic
processes at various spatiotemporal scales.
Weaknesses
1) While the article makes a contribution to the understanding of AMOC dynamics under
LGM conditions, it glosses over important aspects that could refine its conclusions. A key omission
is the lack of detailed discussion on the vertical stratification of the Atlantic Ocean, a mechanism
that plays a critical role in modulating AMOC strength during the glacial period. This gap is
particularly notable given that studies like those of Adkins et al., 2002; Knorr et al., 2021; Chen
et al., 2024 have argued that a stronger stratification during the LGM was a critical factor for the
shoaling of the AMOC. Specifically, they suggest that the salinity of glacial deep waters, which
offset the effect of their warmer temperatures, is crucial for understanding changes in density and,
by extension, the depth and strength of the AMOC. Chen et al. further argue that strong glacial-
ocean stratification, independent of tidal dissipation, was primarily responsible for the shoaled
AMOC during the glacial period. As one aim is to investigate the influences of the abyssal biases
on the AMOC, one might look onto earlier papers analyzing the effect of Southern Ocean
warming (Zhang et al., 2013, CP, also discussing PMIP). Similar sensitivity experiments under
the LGM boundary with restoring were already performed earlier, but it is not mentioned. Indeed,
a salty deep ocean is found to be a prerequisite for glacial termination (Knorr et al., 2021, Nat
Geo), see also Extended Data Fig. 10: Glacial Atlantic salinity structure in models of the last three
PMIP/CMIP generations.
Response:
The suggested references and discussion are added to the text.
2) Moreover, the paper does not engage deeply with the interactions between different
ocean basins, particularly the Atlantic and Indo-Pacific. While the correlation between the
Southern Ocean wind-driven and Indo-Pacific diffusive pathways is presented, there is limited
discussion of the mechanisms by which these pathways interact to influence the AMOC. Given
the complex nature of ocean circulation, particularly in the Southern Ocean, a more detailed treatment
of how these processes interlink would strengthen the authors' argument. My feeling is that this
aspect is the truly innovative one.
Response:
The influences of the different pathways on the AMOC can be summarised as follows:
a) The Southern Ocean wind-driven pathway is primarily dependent on the westerly surface
winds. Intensified westerly winds exist in the glacial and warm climates (Extended Figure 4),
which strengthens the AMOC.
b) At the present-day climate, the Indo-Pacific and the Atlantic basin are linked via the Indian
Ocean inflow, resulting from shallower mid-depth isopycnal depth in the Atlantic. During the
warm state, such link is weakened due to reduced inter-basin transport caused by strong upper-
ocean stratification induced by surface warming and freshening.
c) The opposing changes induced by cooling and salinification leads to large uncertainties in
the upper ocean stratification and a highly variable Indo-Pacific pathway during the LGM. The
glacial AMOC is the result of a strengthening Southern Ocean pathway and a variable Indo-Pacific
pathway, and hence subject to large uncertainty.
d) Moreover, mesoscale processes may have significant contributions to the inter-basin
transport and hence the AMOC via the salt-advection feedback as revealed by eddy-permitting
models (e.g., Biastoch et al., 2009).
The discussion is added to the text as suggested. Please refer to the revised manuscript for
details.
3) As a more minor Conceptual Gaps and Uncertainties: 3) The authors’ reliance on
model correlations to constrain AMOC strength is also problematic because it assumes that the
relationships observed in modern climate states are fully transferable to the glacial period. The
LGM represents a unique set of conditions—such as the presence of large ice sheets, altered
atmospheric circulation patterns, and reduced CO₂ concentrations—that may have influenced
AMOC dynamics in ways that are not captured by present-day pathways. This introduces an
additional layer of uncertainty that is not fully addressed.

In conclusion, while the article provides a contribution to our understanding of the AMOC
under different climate states, it is limited by its under-exploration of vertical stratification in the
Atlantic Ocean, its reliance on uncertain present-day analogs for constraining glacial AMOC
strength, and its insufficient treatment of the interactions between different ocean basins. The study
would benefit from a deeper examination of these processes, particularly the role of glacial
ocean stratification (some references are given above) and interbasin linkages, to provide a more
comprehensive and accurate picture of AMOC variability across past, present, and future climate
states.
